stages.title: Tokenizer
stages.summary: Splits raw text into word tokens, keeping punctuation separate.

stages.title: Part-of-speech tagger
stages.summary: Tags every token with a lexical category (NN, VBZ, IN, ...). These become the leaves of the tree.

items.example: my, your, his, her, its, their

stages.title: Constituency parser
stages.summary: Groups tokens into phrase nodes (NP, VP, PP, ...) bottom-up until one root node spans the sentence.

stages.title: Rule matrix (SynTutor)
stages.summary: SynTutor's own analysis: walks the tree and fires grammar constraints. Each maps to a numbered rule.

items.name: Regular noun plurals
items.concept: Most English nouns form the plural by adding -s (or -es after s, x, z, ch, sh), so "box" becomes "boxes", not "boxs".

items.name: Irregular noun plurals
items.concept: Some nouns have irregular plurals that are not formed with -s: "child → children", "mouse → mice", "man → men".

items.name: Possessive ‘s / s’
items.concept: A possessive shows ownership with 's (singular) or s' (plural already ending in -s): "the boy's toy", "the boys' toys".

items.name: Verb endings (-s, -ed, -ing)
items.concept: Verb endings must match their use: -s for third-person singular, -ed for past, -ing after be or as a gerund; spelling changes can apply ("run → running").

items.name: Irregular past tense
items.concept: Many common verbs have irregular past-tense forms ("go → went", "take → took") that are not made by adding -ed.

items.name: Irregular past participle
items.concept: With have/had, the past participle is required; irregular verbs often differ from the past tense ("had gone", not "had went").

items.name: Comparative/superlative formation
items.concept: Comparatives and superlatives use -er/-est for short adjectives and more/most for longer ones — not both ("taller" or "more tall", never "more taller").

items.name: Adverb formation
items.concept: An adverb is normally formed from an adjective with -ly ("happy → happily"); some adjectives already end in -ly and stay unchanged.

items.name: Reflexive forms
items.concept: Reflexive pronouns end in -self/-selves and must match the subject ("himself", "yourself"), never non-standard forms like "hisself".

items.name: Homophones (its/it’s, their/there)
items.concept: Homophones sound alike but differ in meaning and spelling: "its" (possessive) vs "it’s" (it is), "their"/"there"/"they’re".

items.name: Contractions
items.concept: A contraction replaces missing letters with an apostrophe ("do not → don’t", "I am → I’m"); dropping the apostrophe changes the word.

items.name: Spelling
items.concept: English spelling is not fully predictable, so some words must be learned ("receive", "necessary", "separate").

items.name: Numerals and measures
items.concept: Numbers and measures have fixed patterns: hundred/thousand stay singular after a numeral ("two hundred", not "two hundreds"); units follow the noun.

items.name: Subject-verb, simple
items.concept: A verb must agree in number with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb ("The boy goes"), a plural subject a plural verb.

items.name: Subject-verb, simple
items.concept: A verb must agree in number with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb ("The boy goes"), a plural subject a plural verb.

items.name: Subject-verb, simple
items.concept: A verb must agree in number with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb ("The boy goes"), a plural subject a plural verb.

items.name: Subject-verb, simple
items.concept: A verb must agree in number with its subject: a singular subject takes a singular verb ("The boy goes"), a plural subject a plural verb.

items.name: Subject-verb across intervening phrase
items.example: The boy with the bags go
items.concept: Agreement ignores phrases between the subject and verb, so the verb matches the head noun, not the nearest noun ("The boy with the bags goes").

items.name: Coordinated subjects (and / or / nor)
items.concept: With subjects joined by "and" the verb is plural; with "or"/"nor" it agrees with the nearer subject ("Tom or Ann is").

items.name: Coordinated subjects (and / or / nor)
items.concept: With subjects joined by "and" the verb is plural; with "or"/"nor" it agrees with the nearer subject ("Tom or Ann is").

items.name: Existential there
items.concept: In "there is/are", the verb agrees with the following noun, not with "there" ("There are books").

items.name: Existential there
items.concept: In "there is/are", the verb agrees with the following noun, not with "there" ("There are books").

items.name: Collective and notional nouns
items.concept: Collective and notional nouns can take a singular or plural verb depending on whether the group is treated as one unit or several members.

items.name: Questions and inversion
items.concept: In questions the verb agrees with the subject and appears after the interrogative word ("Where are the books?").

items.name: Relative clauses
items.concept: Inside a relative clause the verb agrees with the relative pronoun’s antecedent ("the boys who play", not "who plays").

items.name: Relative clauses
items.concept: Inside a relative clause the verb agrees with the relative pronoun’s antecedent ("the boys who play", not "who plays").

items.name: Relative clauses
items.concept: Inside a relative clause the verb agrees with the relative pronoun’s antecedent ("the boys who play", not "who plays").

items.name: Indefinite pronouns
items.concept: Indefinite pronouns like everyone, somebody, each take a singular verb ("Everyone has").

items.name: Indefinite pronouns
items.concept: Indefinite pronouns like everyone, somebody, each take a singular verb ("Everyone has").

items.name: Quantified subjects
items.example: A number of / Each of the boys are
items.concept: Quantified subjects agree according to the head: "each/a number of" patterns determine singular or plural ("Each of the boys is").

items.name: Determiner-noun number
items.concept: Demonstratives must match noun number: "this/that" with singular, "these/those" with plural ("these books").

items.name: Quantifier-noun
items.concept: Quantifiers pair with the right noun type: "much/little" with uncountable, "many/few" with countable ("less water", "fewer books").

items.name: Quantifier-noun
items.concept: Quantifiers pair with the right noun type: "much/little" with uncountable, "many/few" with countable ("less water", "fewer books").

items.name: Pronoun-antecedent
items.concept: A pronoun must match its antecedent in number and gender ("The girls lost their bags").

items.name: Correlatives
items.concept: With correlatives (either...or, neither...nor) the verb agrees with the nearer subject ("Either he or I am").

items.name: Reflexive-antecedent
items.concept: A reflexive pronoun must refer back to the subject of the clause ("She hurt herself").

items.name: a/an choice
items.concept: Use "an" before a vowel sound and "a" before a consonant sound ("an apple", "a house").

items.name: Missing article
items.concept: Singular countable nouns need a determiner in most contexts ("I saw a dog"), unless the meaning is generic or indefinite plural.

items.name: Unnecessary article
items.concept: Do not add an article before activities, sports, or generic plurals ("She plays football", not "the football").

items.name: Definite vs indefinite
items.concept: Use "the" for something already known or specific, and "a/an" for first mention or one of many.

items.name: Stacked determiners
items.concept: Only one central determiner is allowed per noun phrase — do not stack them ("my book", not "the my book").

items.name: Determiner with no noun
items.concept: A determiner must modify a noun; it cannot stand alone without one ("the my" is incomplete).

items.name: Determiner with no noun
items.concept: A determiner must modify a noun; it cannot stand alone without one ("the my" is incomplete).

items.name: some/any
items.concept: Use "some" mainly in positive statements and "any" in questions and negatives ("I don’t have any money").

items.name: each/every/all/whole/other/another
items.concept: Distributive determiners match noun number and meaning: "each/every" + singular, "another" + singular, "other/all" + plural.

items.name: Countable vs uncountable
items.concept: Uncountable nouns have no plural and take no "a/an" ("information", "advice"), unlike countable nouns ("a fact", "two facts").

items.name: Noun as modifier (number)
items.concept: When a noun modifies another noun it usually stays singular ("a ten-year plan", "a shoe shop").

items.name: Noun as modifier (number)
items.concept: When a noun modifies another noun it usually stays singular ("a ten-year plan", "a shoe shop").

items.name: Noun as modifier (number)
items.concept: When a noun modifies another noun it usually stays singular ("a ten-year plan", "a shoe shop").

items.name: Plural-only / singular -s nouns
items.concept: Some nouns are plural-only ("scissors", "trousers") and some look plural but are singular ("the news is").

items.name: Case, simple
items.example: Me go, between you and I
items.concept: Pronouns change form by grammatical role: subject ("I", "he") vs object ("me", "him"), including after prepositions and "between".

items.name: Case, simple
items.example: Me go, between you and I
items.concept: Pronouns change form by grammatical role: subject ("I", "he") vs object ("me", "him"), including after prepositions and "between".

items.name: Case in coordination and comparison
items.example: Me and him went, taller than I
items.concept: In coordinated or compared phrases, keep the pronoun in the case the role requires ("He and I went", not "Me and him went").

items.name: Ambiguous reference
items.concept: A pronoun should refer clearly to one antecedent; if two nouns could be meant, the reference is ambiguous and should be rewritten.

items.name: Relative pronoun choice
items.concept: Choose the relative pronoun by the antecedent: "who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for either in restrictive clauses.

items.name: Relative pronoun choice
items.concept: Choose the relative pronoun by the antecedent: "who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for either in restrictive clauses.

items.name: Relative pronoun choice
items.concept: Choose the relative pronoun by the antecedent: "who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for either in restrictive clauses.

items.name: Relative pronoun choice
items.concept: Choose the relative pronoun by the antecedent: "who" for people, "which" for things, "that" for either in restrictive clauses.

items.name: Dummy it/there
items.concept: Dummy "it"/"there" must be present where English requires a subject ("It is raining", not "Is raining").

items.name: Possessive pronoun vs determiner
items.concept: A possessive determiner ("my") needs a following noun; a possessive pronoun ("mine") stands alone ("This is mine", not "This is my").

items.name: Reflexive vs ordinary pronoun
items.concept: A reflexive pronoun cannot be the subject of a finite clause; use an ordinary pronoun ("I am happy", not "Myself am happy").

items.name: Auxiliary + verb form
items.concept: After an auxiliary or modal, use the required form: base form after modals ("can go"), past participle after have, -ing after be.

items.name: Auxiliary + verb form
items.concept: After an auxiliary or modal, use the required form: base form after modals ("can go"), past participle after have, -ing after be.

items.name: Auxiliary + verb form
items.concept: After an auxiliary or modal, use the required form: base form after modals ("can go"), past participle after have, -ing after be.

items.name: Auxiliary + verb form
items.concept: After an auxiliary or modal, use the required form: base form after modals ("can go"), past participle after have, -ing after be.

items.name: Finite main verb
items.concept: A main clause needs a finite verb (tensed and agreeing), not a bare -ing or infinitive with no auxiliary ("She goes to school").

items.name: Finite main verb
items.concept: A main clause needs a finite verb (tensed and agreeing), not a bare -ing or infinitive with no auxiliary ("She goes to school").

items.name: Missing verb / copula
items.concept: English clauses need a verb, including the copula "be"; adjectives cannot stand alone as predicates ("She is very happy").

items.name: Missing verb / copula
items.concept: English clauses need a verb, including the copula "be"; adjectives cannot stand alone as predicates ("She is very happy").

items.name: Passive formation
items.concept: A passive is formed with be + past participle ("The house was built"), not the bare base form.

items.name: Intransitive passive
items.concept: Intransitive verbs (happen, arrive, sleep) have no passive because they take no object ("It happened", not "It was happened").

items.name: Stative verbs in progressive
items.concept: Stative verbs (know, like, believe) describe states and are not normally used in the progressive ("I know", not "I am knowing").

items.name: Stative verbs in progressive
items.concept: Stative verbs (know, like, believe) describe states and are not normally used in the progressive ("I know", not "I am knowing").

items.name: Tense consistency
items.concept: Keep tense and logic consistent across a sentence or narrative ("He said he would come").

items.name: Transitivity
items.concept: Verbs take the complements their meaning allows; some need no preposition ("discuss", not "discuss about").

items.name: Gerund vs infinitive
items.concept: Some verbs are followed by a gerund, some by an infinitive, and some by both with a change in meaning ("enjoy swimming").

items.name: Gerund vs infinitive
items.concept: Some verbs are followed by a gerund, some by an infinitive, and some by both with a change in meaning ("enjoy swimming").

items.name: to + base form
items.concept: After the infinitive marker "to" use the base form ("to go", not "to goes").

items.name: to + base form
items.concept: After the infinitive marker "to" use the base form ("to go", not "to goes").

items.name: to + base form
items.concept: After the infinitive marker "to" use the base form ("to go", not "to goes").

items.name: Phrasal verbs
items.concept: A phrasal verb keeps its particle next to it, and a pronoun object must go between verb and particle ("pick it up").

items.name: Phrasal verbs
items.concept: A phrasal verb keeps its particle next to it, and a pronoun object must go between verb and particle ("pick it up").

items.name: Modals and semi-modals
items.example: must to go, use to go
items.concept: Modals take the bare base form and add no "-s" or "-ed" ("must go", not "must to go").

items.name: Modals and semi-modals
items.example: must to go, use to go
items.concept: Modals take the bare base form and add no "-s" or "-ed" ("must go", not "must to go").

items.name: Question formation
items.concept: Yes/no and wh- questions invert the subject and auxiliary ("Where are you going?").

items.name: Negation
items.concept: Standard English uses a single negative; use "any" rather than a second "no" ("I don’t have any money").

items.name: Imperatives
items.concept: Imperatives use the base form with no subject and no "-s" ("Go!", not "Goes!").

items.name: Conditionals
items.concept: In real conditionals use present tense in the if-clause, not "will" ("If I go, I will see him").

items.name: Subjunctive and wish
items.concept: After "wish" and in the subjunctive, use the past or base form for hypotheticals ("I wish I were here").

items.name: Reported speech
items.concept: Reported speech shifts tense and uses "tell + person" or "say + clause" ("She told me", not "She said me").

items.name: Causatives and perception verbs
items.concept: Causative and perception verbs take specific structures: "make/let + base", "have/get + past participle", "see + base/-ing".

items.name: Verb + clause patterns
items.concept: Different verbs select different clause patterns ("suggest going", "advise someone to go"), so the complement must match the verb.

items.name: Verb + clause patterns
items.concept: Different verbs select different clause patterns ("suggest going", "advise someone to go"), so the complement must match the verb.

items.name: Adjective vs adverb
items.concept: Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Use the adverb after an action verb ("runs quickly").

items.name: Adjective vs adverb
items.concept: Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Use the adverb after an action verb ("runs quickly").

items.name: Adjective vs adverb

items.name: Adjective vs adverb
items.concept: Adjectives modify nouns; adverbs modify verbs, adjectives, or other adverbs. Use the adverb after an action verb ("runs quickly").

items.name: Adjective order
items.concept: When several adjectives stack, English fixes their order: opinion, size, age, shape, colour, origin, material, purpose.

items.name: Adverb placement
items.concept: Adverbs of frequency and degree have preferred positions and usually cannot split a verb and its object.

items.name: Participial adjectives
items.concept: Participial adjectives differ: "-ing" describes the cause ("boring"), "-ed" describes the feeler ("bored").

items.name: Intensifiers and degree
items.concept: Degree words combine with the right adjective and position: "big enough", "very good", "too big" — not "enough big".

items.name: Comparative structures
items.concept: Form comparatives once: either -er/-est or more/most, and use "than" for comparison ("taller than").

items.name: Comparative structures

items.name: Modifier position
items.concept: English puts most modifiers before the noun; reversing the order ("the car red") is ungrammatical.

items.name: Modifier position

items.name: Wrong preposition
items.concept: The preposition a verb or adjective takes is fixed by convention ("depend on", not "depend in").

items.name: Wrong preposition

items.name: Wrong preposition

items.name: Missing preposition
items.concept: Some verbs require a preposition to introduce their object ("listen to music", not "listen music").

items.name: Unnecessary preposition
items.concept: Some verbs already include the meaning of the preposition, so adding one is wrong ("discuss the plan").

items.name: Adjective + preposition
items.concept: Adjective + preposition pairs are fixed ("interested in", "good at", "afraid of").

items.name: Time and place (in/on/at)
items.concept: Time and place prepositions follow set patterns: "at" a point, "on" a day/date, "in" a period/area.

items.name: Time and place (in/on/at)
items.concept: Time and place prepositions follow set patterns: "at" a point, "on" a day/date, "in" a period/area.

items.name: Time and place (in/on/at)
items.concept: Time and place prepositions follow set patterns: "at" a point, "on" a day/date, "in" a period/area.

items.name: Preposition + gerund
items.concept: A preposition is followed by a noun or a gerund ("look forward to seeing"), not a bare infinitive.

items.name: Fragment
items.concept: A sentence needs at least one independent clause; a subordinate clause alone is a fragment ("Because I was late" cannot stand alone).

items.name: Fragment
items.concept: A sentence needs at least one independent clause; a subordinate clause alone is a fragment ("Because I was late" cannot stand alone).

items.name: Missing subject
items.concept: A finite clause needs a subject; leaving it out produces a fragment ("I went to school").

items.name: Run-on / fused sentence
items.example: I like tea she likes coffee
items.concept: Two independent clauses cannot sit side by side without a conjunction or punctuation ("I like tea, but she likes coffee").

items.name: Comma splice
items.concept: A comma alone cannot join two independent clauses; use a conjunction, a semicolon, or a full stop.

items.name: Double subject
items.concept: Do not give the subject twice with a pronoun ("My brother went", not "My brother he went").

items.name: Word order in statements
items.concept: Statements use subject-before-verb order; inverted order belongs only to questions ("Yesterday I went").

items.name: Missing or extra word
items.concept: A clause should carry exactly the words it needs; extras or omissions break the structure ("She is very happy").

items.name: Parallel structure
items.concept: Items in a list or comparison must share the same grammatical form ("to run and to swim", not "to run and swimming").

items.name: Parallel structure
items.concept: Items in a list or comparison must share the same grammatical form ("to run and to swim", not "to run and swimming").

items.name: Conjunction pairing
items.concept: Correlative conjunctions come in fixed pairs; do not add a second connector ("Although X, Y" without "but").

items.name: Relative clause formation
items.example: the man who I saw him
items.concept: A relative clause already contains the role of the antecedent, so do not repeat it with a pronoun ("the man who I saw").

items.name: Relative clause formation
items.example: the man who I saw him
items.concept: A relative clause already contains the role of the antecedent, so do not repeat it with a pronoun ("the man who I saw").

items.name: Dangling / misplaced modifier
items.concept: A modifier at the start of a sentence should describe the subject of the main clause ("Walking home, I saw the rain start").

items.name: Redundancy
items.concept: Avoid redundant words that repeat meaning ("return", not "return back").

items.name: Indirect question word order
items.concept: An embedded question keeps statement word order ("I wonder where he is").

items.name: Indirect question word order
items.concept: An embedded question keeps statement word order ("I wonder where he is").

items.name: Clause linking
items.concept: Link clauses with the structure each connector requires ("because I wanted to see you").

items.name: Object order
items.concept: Give the direct and indirect object in the standard order, or use the right preposition ("give me a book", "give a book to me").

items.name: Object order

items.name: Sentence-initial capital
items.concept: Begin every sentence with a capital letter.

items.name: Sentence-initial capital
items.concept: Begin every sentence with a capital letter.

items.name: Proper nouns, “I”, days, months
items.concept: Capitalise proper nouns, the pronoun "I", and the names of days and months.

items.name: Proper nouns, “I”, days, months
items.concept: Capitalise proper nouns, the pronoun "I", and the names of days and months.

items.name: Terminal punctuation
items.concept: End a declarative or imperative sentence with a full stop, a question with "?" and a strong exclamation with "!".

items.name: Commas
items.concept: Commas separate list items, mark introductory phrases, and set off non-essential clauses — but they cannot join two main clauses.

items.name: Apostrophes
items.concept: Apostrophes mark possession and contraction, not ordinary plurals ("the 1990s").

items.name: Quotation and dialogue
items.concept: Quotation marks must be opened and closed around the exact words, with punctuation placed correctly.

items.name: Hyphens and dashes
items.concept: Use hyphens to join compound modifiers before a noun ("a well-known author") and dashes for breaks in a sentence.

items.name: Colons and semicolons
items.concept: Use a colon to introduce a list or explanation and a semicolon to join closely related independent clauses.

items.name: Spacing and repeats
items.concept: Use single spaces between words and avoid accidental repeated words ("the the").

items.name: Numbers, dates, abbreviations
items.concept: Follow consistent conventions for numbers, dates, and abbreviations within a text.

items.name: Confusable words
items.concept: Confusable words sound or look alike but differ in meaning or part of speech ("affect" = verb, "effect" = noun).

items.name: Collocations
items.concept: Collocations are word partnerships fixed by convention ("make a decision", not "do a decision").

items.name: Tense-time agreement
items.concept: The tense must match the time expressed by adverbs such as "yesterday" ("Yesterday I went").

items.name: Tense-time agreement
items.concept: The tense must match the time expressed by adverbs such as "yesterday" ("Yesterday I went").

items.name: Selectional restrictions
items.concept: A verb’s meaning restricts what can be its subject or object ("The book eats" is impossible).

items.name: Structural ambiguity
items.concept: Some sentences have more than one possible structure; the intended meaning should be made explicit.

items.name: Register
items.concept: Register should match the situation: slang and casual forms do not belong in formal writing.

items.name: L1 interference / false friends
items.concept: First-language patterns can produce errors in English ("I am agree" from "estoy de acuerdo"); use the English structure.

items.name: Connector misuse
items.example: I was tired, however I slept
items.concept: Connectors express a specific logical relation, so the one chosen must match the meaning ("I was tired, so I slept").
